CONDITIONAL: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 10, audited at commit c6b238b (committed; working tree carries only
sprint bookkeeping). Sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict,
including the 16 Aug rewrite for anonymous link-addressed readings.

VERDICT: CONDITIONAL PASS. One required fix. It is not a style point -- as committed,
this sprint cannot ship, because CI will go red before the migration ever runs.

REQUIRED FIX -- Sprint 4's RLS suite is broken by this sprint's migration, and
nothing has run it yet to notice.

The migration adds:

    alter table public.readings add column positions jsonb not null;

No default. Meanwhile supabase/tests/rls.test.ts -- untouched by this sprint, I
checked the diff -- still builds its rows from:

    function validReading(overrides = {}) {
      return { event_date, place_name, latitude, longitude, timezone, ...overrides };
    }

There is no `positions` key. Every insert that helper feeds now violates a NOT NULL
constraint. Concretely:

  - the `readings RLS policies` describe block's beforeAll insert throws
    "setup insert failed: null value in column \"positions\" ... violates not-null
    constraint", which takes down all six tests under it;
  - the "can insert a reading" test fails on its own account.

Both files run in the same `npm run test:rls` invocation (vitest.rls.config.ts
includes supabase/tests/**), which is the rls-tests job, which migrate declares in
`needs`. So the chain is: rls-tests fails -> migrate is skipped -> `supabase db push`
never runs -> the deploy hook never fires -> nothing reaches production. Sprint 4's
gate and Sprint 5's ordering both work exactly as designed here; what they are
catching is this.

Fix: add a positions value to validReading (the fixture in this sprint's own
readings-save-retrieve.test.ts is a fine shape to copy). The place columns can stay
-- the migration relaxed their NOT NULL rather than dropping them, so they remain
valid input.

I could not execute this: no Docker on this machine, so no local stack and no
PostgREST, same limitation I have flagged since Sprint 4. But the mechanism is not in
doubt -- a NOT NULL column with no default and an insert that omits it is a
constraint violation, not a judgement call. CI on the first push would have found it;
that is a slower and more expensive place to find it than here.

Requirements coverage:
R1 MET. New timestamped migration, no DDL outside supabase/migrations/, and no
  destructive change: the four vestigial place columns have their NOT NULL relaxed
  rather than being dropped, which is a widening and therefore expand-then-contract
  compliant. The comment explaining why they are relaxed rather than dropped -- a
  constraint nothing can satisfy would fail every insert -- is exactly right, and
  catching that at all is the kind of thing that gets missed. See note 5 on the
  contract half.
R2 MET. crypto.randomUUID(), a CSPRNG, generated server-side in the action. The
  comment explaining why the id is chosen before the write rather than read back from
  it -- there is no SELECT policy, so `insert ... returning` comes back empty even on
  success -- shows the Sprint 4 design was carried forward deliberately rather than
  rediscovered by trial and error.
R3 MET, and I checked it as the direct grep the criterion asked for. The readings
  feature uses createAnonClient() exclusively. The only service-role reference
  anywhere in app/ or lib/ is app/api/health/db/route.ts, which is Sprint 2's health
  endpoint reading schema_migrations, touches no readings row, and is not part of
  this feature. supabase/tests/readings-save-retrieve.test.ts builds its client from
  resolvePublicConfig too -- no service role key in the test path either, which is
  where a vacuous pass would have hidden.
R4 MET. app/reading/[id]/page.tsx renders a stored reading for anyone holding the
  link, with no session or cookie involved.
R5 MET, verified by enumeration rather than by trusting the guardrail. I listed every
  readings query in the tree at c6b238b: exactly two exist -- an insert in
  app/chart/actions.ts with no trailing .select(), and the get_reading_by_id RPC in
  the reading page. There is no listing route, handler, or query. See note 1 for how
  much the accompanying test actually protects that going forward.
R6 MET, and the test proving it is better than it needed to be. The reading page
  reads data[0] from the RPC and renders it; nothing recomputes. The round-trip test
  deliberately stores fixture positions that are NOT what a real computation for
  1999-08-11 would produce, so an exact match on read proves stored data rather than
  the ephemeris adapter running again. That is the difference between a test that
  passes and a test that discriminates.
R7 MET. The insert error is checked and redirects back to /chart with a message; the
  user never sees a success state for a failed write, and never lands on a
  /reading/<id> for a row that was not written. Confirmed live that /chart renders
  the reflected error in a role="alert" paragraph. See note 3 -- the error is
  surfaced but not recorded anywhere.
R8 MET, all four cases with real assertions: round trip; random unguessed id returns
  an empty result; no listing route (lib/readings-access-guardrail.test.ts); and a
  save failure surfacing an error (a deliberate NOT NULL violation). None of them can
  currently run -- see the required fix.

Verified by execution:
- lint, typecheck, default test suite: all exit 0, 65 tests across 7 files. Note that
  the default suite excludes supabase/tests/, which is exactly why the breakage above
  does not show up locally.
- next build exits 0; /reading/[id] is a dynamic route, as it must be.
- Rebuilt with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY="QA1PROBESERVICEROLE" and grepped all of
  .next: absent from the entire build output.
- Live against the built app: /chart?date=2024-03-20 renders the "Save this reading"
  form; a reflected ?error= value renders in role="alert"; /reading/<uuid> and
  /reading/not-a-uuid both return 404 rather than a 500 or a stack trace.

Notes, not conditions:
1. The R5 guardrail is weaker than it reads, and I demonstrated both gaps against the
   real tree rather than asserting them:
     - hasUnscopedReadingsSelect operates on the WHOLE FILE. Any file containing
       "get_reading_by_id" or `.eq("id"` anywhere is exempt in its entirety. I added
       `createAnonClient().from("readings").select("*")` to app/reading/[id]/page.tsx
       -- which contains the RPC -- and the guardrail test still PASSED.
     - findUnfilteredReadingsQueries only walks app/. I put the listing query in
       lib/list-readings.ts and called it from a new app/admin-list/page.tsx: a
       complete, working route returning every reading. The guardrail test PASSED.
   R5 and R8 are both met -- the code has no listing query today and the test does
   assert something real -- so this is not a condition. But the sprint's own risk
   register says a listing endpoint "converts unguessable links into a public index in
   one commit", and hole 2 is precisely that commit, staying green. Walking lib/ as
   well as app/, and applying the exemptions per call rather than per file, closes
   both.
2. A Supabase outage is indistinguishable from a deleted reading. app/reading/[id]
   collapses `error`, null data, and an empty result into notFound(); I confirmed
   live that with an unreachable Supabase host every reading link returns 404. The
   uniformity between a malformed id and a nonexistent id is correct and the comment
   defends it well -- those two must look identical from outside. A transport failure
   is a different thing, it is not id-dependent, and distinguishing it leaks nothing
   about which ids exist. For a product whose entire proposition is "this link keeps
   working", a saved reading appearing permanently deleted during an outage is worth
   two lines to avoid.
3. Nothing on the write path is logged. app/chart/actions.ts discards the Supabase
   error object entirely and redirects with a fixed string; the reading page discards
   its error too. R7 is satisfied -- the user is told -- but during an incident there
   would be nothing anywhere saying why saves are failing. This is the same swallow I
   raised on Sprint 6, and it matters more here because it is a write path. One
   console.error in each branch lands in Vercel's logs.
4. `positions` is unvalidated on read. The page casts the jsonb straight to
   StoredReading and calls .map() and .toFixed() on it. Sprint 4's insert policy is
   `with check (true)`, so any anon client can write arbitrary jsonb into that column
   -- a row whose positions is a string or an object makes that link throw a 500. It
   is self-inflicted (the attacker can only craft a link they already hold) so this
   is low, but an Array.isArray guard falling through to notFound() is two lines.
5. The four place columns are now nullable, unused, and permanently present. That is
   the correct call this sprint -- R1 forbids the destructive change -- but it is the
   expand half of expand-then-contract with no contract half scheduled, and this is
   the final sprint. Either drop them in a follow-up migration or write down that
   they are knowingly left behind, so the next person does not have to work out
   whether they mean anything.
6. Accepted, not raised as a defect: the public write path has no rate limiting, and
   since Sprint 5 previews share the production database. Anyone can write unlimited
   rows to production readings through a public form. The sprint file names this
   explicitly as out of scope so its absence is a decision. Noting it here so the
   record shows the gate saw it and agreed rather than missed it.

Re-audit after the rls.test.ts fixture fix. It is one key in one object; keep the
re-audit proportionate to that. Nothing else in this diff needs to move.

PASS: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 10, round 2. Audited at commit 92f532f, covering b13829d (the

REQUIRED FIX -- validReading() supplies positions. FIXED (b13829d), three lines, one
file. All three insert paths into readings now supply the column: validReading(), the
round-trip fixture, and app/chart/actions.ts. The place columns staying in the

AUTHORIZED SCOPE ADDITION -- the no-listing-route guardrail. FIXED (92f532f), and I
verified it the same way I found the holes: by re-running both mutations against the
real tree rather than reading the new logic and believing it.

  hole 1, unfiltered select added to the file that already contains the RPC
    round 1: guardrail PASSED (hole open)
    now:     guardrail FAILED  <- caught

  hole 2, listing query in lib/list-readings.ts called from app/admin-list/page.tsx
    round 1: guardrail PASSED (hole open)
    now:     guardrail FAILED  <- caught

Both closed. The implementation does the two things that actually matter: the
exemption now lives on the same statement as the danger rather than anywhere in the
same file, and findUnfilteredReadingsQueries takes a list of roots so lib/ is walked
alongside app/. Excluding the detector module by name rather than by some clever
self-reference test is the right call -- it means nobody has to re-argue
self-exclusion every time that file changes.

What lifts this above a minimal fix: both holes now have regression tests that write
real fixture trees into tmpdir and run the real walk over them, not just string-level
unit cases. A logic change that reopens either hole fails a test that names it. The
holes cannot quietly come back, which is the part a fix usually leaves out.

Requirements coverage: round 1's findings stand unchanged, R1 through R8 all met. I

Note 5 from round 1 is closed as a documented decision rather than a code change: the
README now states the four place columns are vestigial, nullable rather than dropped,

Notes, not conditions:
1. NEW, and a residual limit rather than a regression: splitting the query builder
   across two statements still evades the guardrail. I probed it after the fix:

     const q = createAnonClient().from("readings");
     const { data } = await q.select("*");

   in an app/ route -- guardrail PASSES. The first chunk names readings but has no
   .select(; the second has .select( but does not name readings. This is inherent to
   splitting on `;` rather than parsing, it is not something the fix introduced, and
   the module says so directly in the comment above statementChunks rather than
   implying more rigour than it has. Closing it properly means an AST pass, which is
   not a change worth making on the last commit of the exercise. Recording it so the
   guardrail's actual reach is on the record: it catches the realistic shape -- a
   debug listing endpoint written as one fluent chain, anywhere in app/ or lib/ --
   and does not catch a deliberately split one. Nobody should read the green test as
   proof that no listing query can exist.
2. Carried from round 1, unchanged and still open, all deferred with my agreement:
   a Supabase outage renders as 404 on every reading link, indistinguishable from a
   deleted reading (the malformed-id/nonexistent-id uniformity is correct and should
   stay; a transport error is not id-dependent and distinguishing it leaks nothing);
   nothing on the write path is logged, so an incident would leave no record of why
   saves are failing; readings.positions is cast to StoredReading and mapped without
   an Array.isArray guard, so a crafted row 500s its own link; and the public write
   path has no rate limiting against a database previews share, which the sprint file
   names as an accepted decision.

STILL NOT EXECUTED, and this is the sentence that matters most in the closing sprint:
nothing under supabase/tests/ has ever run. Not the save-and-retrieve round trip, not
the unguessed-id case, not the deliberate save-failure case, and not Sprint 4's RLS
suite either before or after the fixture fix that unbroke it. No Docker on this
machine, so no local stack and no PostgREST, exactly as I have flagged since Sprint 4.
The required fix above is a reading of Postgres NOT NULL semantics against an
untouched test file, and it is correct, but its correctness will be demonstrated for
the first time by CI on Pipeman's push -- the rls-tests job, which migrate depends on,
which the deploy hook depends on. If that job goes red, that is the pipeline telling
you something real, not a flake. GroundTruth's closing proof on production is where
the whole stack is finally shown to hold together, and it has not been shown yet.

Cleared to ship at 92f532f. Standing note for Pipeman: files under docs/sprints/ are

PASS: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 10, round 3. Audited at commit 5b4ffb9, scoped to that commit --
b13829d and 92f532f passed in round 2 and git diff 92f532f..5b4ffb9 touches only two
migration files, nothing else. Sprint file re-read fresh, byte-identical to rounds 1
and 2 (md5 a4ebde9152ef05b23e975c1f60738867).

VERDICT: PASS.

FIRST, MY OWN ERROR, because it caused this round.

R1's requirement text says the migration must obey Sprint 5's expand-then-contract
rule. I evaluated that rule only against the four vestigial place columns, concluded
correctly that relaxing their NOT NULL is a widening, and then accepted
`add column positions jsonb not null` on the strength of a claim written in the
migration's own comment -- "production's readings table has never had a row written
to it." I did not verify that claim. I could not have verified it statically, which
is precisely the reason it should have been flagged as an assumption rather than
absorbed as a fact.

Worse, I had already written the contradiction down myself. My Sprint 5 audit records,
in my own words, that a preview writing data "writes it into the same table
production reads." Sprint 4's GroundTruth criteria require retrieving and attempting
to update an existing production row, which means rows. Both halves were in my own
audit record and I did not join them. The push failing on SQLSTATE 23502 is what
joined them. That is a static-gate miss, not a Dev Team one.

THE FIX. Correct, and correct for the right reason.

  20260816174352 -- `add column positions jsonb` (nullable). Pure expand.
  20260816181929 -- backfill nulls to '[]'::jsonb, then `set not null`. Contract.

Backfilling to an empty array rather than inventing plausible positions is the right
call and the comment says why: those rows never had positions computed, and an empty
array records that honestly. app/reading/[id]/page.tsx maps over positions, so `[]`
renders a header and an empty table rather than throwing -- the claim in the commit
message checks out against the code.

I traced what happens on the next push under all three possible production states,
because the whole justification for editing 20260816174352 in place rests on which
one is true:
  - migration fully rolled back (what the commit asserts): the CLI has no history
    record, so it re-runs the edited file. Correct outcome.
  - migration somehow fully applied: the CLI skips it as already-applied, then
    20260816181929 runs -- its UPDATE matches nothing and its SET NOT NULL is a
    no-op against a column already NOT NULL. Correct outcome, and the drift check
    still matches because the shadow database built from the migration set also ends
    at NOT NULL.
  - migration partially applied (transaction assumption wrong): the four
    `alter column ... drop not null` statements are idempotent, and `add column
    positions jsonb` only errors if the column already exists, which is the
    fully-applied case above.
The fix self-heals in every branch. That robustness is why this is a PASS rather
than a hold on an unverified fact -- see note 1 for the fact I still want checked.

Requirements coverage: round 2's findings stand, R1 through R8 all met. R1 in
particular is now met on the requirement text and not merely on its acceptance
criterion. Re-verified at 5b4ffb9: five migrations, each ending in a ledger insert
whose version string matches its own filename; no DDL anywhere outside
supabase/migrations/; the RLS fixture from b13829d still supplies positions, which
remains valid input against a column that is nullable then tightened.

Verified by execution at 5b4ffb9:
- lint, typecheck, default test suite: all exit 0, 70 tests across 7 files.
- next build exits 0; route table unchanged, four routes, no listing route.
- Rebuilt with SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY="QA1PROBESERVICEROLE" and grepped all of
  .next: absent from the entire build output.

Notes, not conditions:
1. MUST BE CHECKED BEFORE THE RE-PUSH, and I cannot check it -- live verification is
   GroundTruth's job, not mine. The justification for editing a migration in place is
   that it never applied. The evidence offered for that is the Supabase CLI's
   documented transactional behaviour, which is an inference from documentation, not
   an observation of production -- the same class of reasoning that produced the
   "readings has never had a row" error this commit is fixing. It is cheaply
   checkable with the observable Sprint 2 built for exactly this: GET
   /api/health/db on production reports the latest applied migration version. It
   should read 20260816134147_readings_rls_policies. If it reads
   20260816174352_readings_positions, the migration did apply, and someone needs to
   revisit this commit rather than push it. Ten seconds, and it converts the
   load-bearing assumption in this fix into a fact.
2. The commit cites Sprint 4's precedent for editing a migration in place. The
   precedent is not identical and the difference is worth being exact about: Sprint
   4's deleted migration was on no remote at all, which I verified statically at the
   time. This one IS on origin/main -- it was pushed, and its migrate job ran and
   failed. The underlying principle still holds, because the forward-only rule
   protects migrations that have been APPLIED, not ones that have merely been
   published; a git remote applies nothing to a database. So the conclusion is right
   and the reasoning needs one more sentence than it got.
3. Carried from rounds 1 and 2, unchanged, all deferred with my agreement: a Supabase
   outage renders as 404 on every reading link, indistinguishable from a deleted
   reading; nothing on the write path is logged; readings.positions is cast and
   mapped without an Array.isArray guard, which now also covers the backfilled `[]`
   rows harmlessly but would not cover a crafted one; the public write path has no
   rate limiting against a shared database; and the guardrail does not catch a query
   builder deliberately split across two statements.

ON THE LONG-STANDING "NOTHING UNDER supabase/tests/ HAS EVER RUN": that is no longer
true, and it is worth recording. For migrate to have reached `supabase db push` at
all, its `needs: [build, rls-tests]` must both have been satisfied -- so the RLS
suite and the save-and-retrieve round trip did execute against a real local stack,
and did pass, before the migration failed downstream of them. That is the first
actual execution of any of it, it validates b13829d (round 1's required fix) against
a real PostgREST rather than against my reading of NOT NULL semantics, and it means
Sprint 4's gate is doing real work rather than notional work. It also means the two
gates caught this in the right order: the suites went green, and the thing they
cannot see -- production's existing data -- is what stopped the push. That is the
pipeline behaving correctly, not failing.

The migration set has changed since that run, so rls-tests must go green again on the
re-push before any of this counts. And GroundTruth's closing proof on production
remains the only thing that demonstrates the whole stack holds together end to end.

Cleared to ship at 5b4ffb9, with note 1 checked first. Standing note for Pipeman:
files under docs/sprints/ are tracked and the tree is dirty with sprint bookkeeping --
do not fold any of it into the shipped commit, the tree content is what /sprint-ship
compares against this verdict.

PASS: GroundTruth live test, Sprint 10, commit 5b4ffb9cd1eb240d2536aff48b853f1f4c3efa31. Environment: https://my-little-racoon.vercel.app and the production Supabase Data API, 2026-08-16 ~18:40-18:55Z. All checks anonymous: no cookies, no session, no service role key. VERDICT: PASS. All four criteria verified, including the closing proof. Two findings recorded, neither failing a criterion; one of them is a genuine no-JavaScript gap I could not fully resolve without a browser, and I have said so rather than rounding it off. Production is serving the shipped commit: page renders 5b4ffb9. CRITERION 1 -- a date can be entered, a reading saved, and a link returned. PASS. The save is a Next.js server action, exposed as a plain no-JS form (
with hidden $ACTION_ID_407e47aa... and date). I invoked it the way a browser without JavaScript would, by POSTing multipart form data: POST /chart?date=1969-07-20 -> HTTP/2 303, location: /reading/59fbb41d-82a4-4786-83eb-17924d654718 A link is returned, and the id is a uuid rather than anything enumerable. CRITERION 2 -- opening that link in a fresh session with no cookies renders the saved reading correctly. PASS. This is the exercise's closing proof. GET /reading/59fbb41d-82a4-4786-83eb-17924d654718 with no cookie jar, no credentials, no prior request state -> HTTP/2 200, zero Set-Cookie headers, and the full reading rendered server-side: "Reading for 1969-07-20 | Sun Cancer 27.58 No | Moon Libra 3.50 No | Mercury Cancer 25.11 No | Venus Gemini 14.66 No | Mars Sagittarius 2.72 No | Jupiter Libra 0.70 No | Saturn Taurus 8.08 No | Uranus Libra 0.68 No | Neptune Scorpio 26.02 Yes | Pluto Virgo 23.00 No" Every value matches what /chart?date=1969-07-20 rendered before the save, including Neptune's retrograde flag. The round trip is faithful. This is a full pass through Vercel, the server action, Supabase, Sprint 4's RLS policies and the migrated schema, observed from outside by a client that had never touched the system. CRITERION 3 -- a made-up id returns not-found rather than an error page or another reading. PASS on substance. See finding 1 for what a human actually sees. /reading/00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000000 -> HTTP 404 /reading/ -> HTTP 404 /reading/not-a-uuid -> HTTP 404 Correct status, no 500, no stack trace. Critically, no other reading is returned: I grepped the 404 responses for sign names, body names, "positions" and uuid patterns -- 0 hits. The response is 6,536 bytes against 10,296 for a real reading, and carries none of another row's data. CRITERION 4 -- there is no reachable way to list readings. PASS. I went looking rather than confirming the absence of a link. Application routes, all 404: /readings, /reading, /api/readings, /api/reading, /api/chart, /chart/list, /readings.json, /api/readings?limit=10, /sitemap.xml, /robots.txt. (No sitemap and no robots.txt also means no route inventory is published for anyone to walk.) Data API as anon, directly against PostgREST: GET /readings?select=* -> [] GET /readings?select=id&order=created_at.desc&limit=5 -> [] Prefer: count=exact, Range: 0-0 -> content-range: */0 The count leaks nothing either -- it reports 0, not the true row count. Speculative listing RPCs, all 404: get_readings, list_readings, all_readings, get_all_readings, readings. The only reachable function remains get_reading_by_id, which takes a single uuid. R6 PROVEN DECISIVELY -- stored positions are read back as stored, NOT recomputed. This is the requirement a static audit cannot settle and a naive live test would have missed, because a correctly-recomputing page and a correctly-storing page render identically. So I made them differ. Using the anon key, I inserted a row directly with deliberately wrong positions: every one of the ten bodies parked at Capricorn 11.11 degrees, retrograde true, under event_date 1969-07-20 (id 047e8dbd-385c-4ce0-adc3-acbf7bd9856d, insert_status 201). GET /reading/047e8dbd-385c-4ce0-adc3-acbf7bd9856d rendered, verbatim: "Reading for 1969-07-20 | Sun Capricorn 11.11 Yes | Moon Capricorn 11.11 Yes | Mercury Capricorn 11.11 Yes | ..." It rendered the stored nonsense, not the correct 1969-07-20 positions it would have produced by recomputing. R6 holds. Related, from reading the stored row through the anon RPC: positions are stored as a JSON array at full precision (Sun eclipticLongitude 117.58120894825002, degreeInSign 27.581208948250037) and rounded only for display. Nothing is lost on write. R7 VERIFIED -- save failures surface as failures, with no silent loss. POST the save action with date=1699-12-31 -> 303 to /chart?date=1699-12-31&error=Date%20must%20be%20between%201700-01-01%20and%202100-12-31. POST with date=not-a-date -> 303 to /chart?date=not-a-date&error=%22not-a-date%22%20is%20not%20a%20date%20in%20YYYY-MM-DD%20form. Following the redirect renders the message to the user -- "Date must be between 1700-01-01 and 2100-12-31." -- with NO positions table and no reading link. No success state is shown for a write that did not happen, and no row was created. R3 CONSISTENT WITH ANON-ONLY, though not provable from outside. The reading page renders a row that a plain anon SELECT cannot see (criterion 4 shows select returns []), while the anon-callable get_reading_by_id RPC can. That is exactly the shape you would expect if the page uses the anon client through Sprint 4's security definer function. It is consistent with "no service role key in this feature"; it is not proof, since I cannot see server-side code from here. QA1's audit is the gate for that one. FINDING 1 -- the not-found page renders BLANK without JavaScript. Severity: low, but it is a real user-visible gap and it is the one thing here I could not close. The 404 response's server-rendered is empty. The strings "404" and "could not be found" are present in the response, but only inside the streamed RSC script payload, not in any server-rendered markup. My curl does not execute JavaScript, so what I actually observed for a bad link was a page with the site title and nothing else. Contrast with the success path: /reading/ renders its whole table server-side. The asymmetry is specific to the not-found branch. My expectation, flagged clearly as inference and NOT verified: a JavaScript- enabled browser hydrates and shows the standard Next.js "404 | This page could not be found." I have no browser in this session -- no Playwright MCP, no Chrome extension -- so I cannot confirm it, and I am not going to assert it.
